title: Vegetarian, Vegan, and Halal Food in Korea: A Beginner's Guide
html:
Worried that a trip to Korea means every meal will have meat, fish sauce, or pork hiding somewhere? Good news: Korea is getting a lot easier for vegetarian, vegan, and halal travelers every year — you just need to know what to look for. This guide walks you through real options, common traps, and the apps and phrases that make eating out stress-free.

Is Korea Vegetarian, Vegan, and Halal Friendly?

Traditional Korean cooking leans heavily on meat, fish, and fermented seafood, so it was not built with these diets in mind. But things are changing fast: Seoul alone now has more than 100 fully vegan restaurants, plant-based cafes are opening in every trendy neighborhood, and the city government is actively working with restaurants near Itaewon to offer more halal-certified menus for Muslim visitors. You will not struggle to find food — you just have to plan a little, the same way you would in most non-Muslim, meat-loving countries.


Bibimbap (rice with mixed vegetables) is one of the easiest Korean dishes to make vegetarian or vegan — just ask for no egg and no meat. Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Vegetarian and Vegan Options: Temple Food, Rice Bowls, and Cafes

Your best friend here is Korean temple food (사찰음식, sachal-eumsik) — the cuisine Buddhist monks have eaten for centuries. It is naturally plant-based, skips strong flavors like garlic and onion, and is served as a set of small, beautifully arranged dishes. In Seoul, Sanchon in Insadong is a long-running temple food restaurant run by a former monk, serving a full vegan set course (around ₩29,000) that even non-vegetarians love. It is small and popular, so call ahead or ask your hotel to book a table — especially for dinner — rather than just walking in.

Outside of temple food, bibimbap (rice mixed with vegetables, sold almost everywhere) is easy to order vegetarian by asking for "no egg, no meat." Many cafes in neighborhoods like Hongdae and Yeonnam-dong now have fully vegan desserts and milk-alternative drinks (oat or soy milk), and convenience stores such as CU and GS25 sell pre-packaged vegan kimbap (rice rolls) and dumplings with a clear label — handy for a quick, cheap, no-hassle meal between sightseeing stops.


A temple food course at Sanchon, Insadong — dozens of small vegetable dishes with no meat, fish, garlic, or onion. Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Watch Out for Hidden Animal Ingredients

This is the part that catches most beginners off guard: a dish that "looks" vegetarian can still have animal products hiding inside. Many everyday soups and stews are made with anchovy broth (멸치육수), and side dishes called banchan — the small shared plates that come free with every meal — sometimes use fish sauce or tiny shrimp for seasoning, even in dishes that look like plain vegetables. Kimchi, in particular, often contains fish sauce or salted seafood as a flavoring, so it is not automatically vegan.

The safest move is to learn one simple phrase: "고기, 생선, 멸치 들어가요?" ("Gogi, saengseon, myeolchi deureogayo?" — "Does this have meat, fish, or anchovy in it?"). Interestingly, this is not just a tourist problem — a growing number of young Koreans who identify as vegetarian or "flexible vegetarian" ask servers the exact same question, so don't feel awkward doing it. Showing a translated card (many free templates exist online, or just type it into a translation app) works just as well if you're not confident saying it out loud.


A typical spread of banchan side dishes — some may contain anchovy or shrimp seasoning even though they look purely vegetable-based. Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Finding Halal and Muslim-Friendly Food in Seoul

For halal travelers, Itaewon is the neighborhood to know. It is home to Korea's oldest mosque and the largest cluster of halal and Muslim-friendly restaurants in the country, including Turkish, Pakistani, and Middle Eastern kebab and curry spots within easy walking distance of Itaewon Station. Seoul's city government has also been expanding a "Muslim-friendly" certification program for restaurants near the mosque, on top of the smaller number of restaurants that carry full KMF (Korea Muslim Federation) halal certification.

A quick warning: online lists of "halal restaurants in Seoul" are often outdated, and a few restaurants named in older blog posts have since closed or changed hands. Don't rely on any single list, including this one, without double-checking first.


The Seoul Central Mosque rises above the streets of Itaewon, the center of Seoul's halal and Muslim-friendly dining scene. Photo by Brandon Butler (kayakorea) via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Halal Certification, Mosques, and Useful Apps for Any Diet

The Seoul Central Mosque in Itaewon is Korea's first and most well-known mosque, and it is worth visiting even just to see the neighborhood around it. For current, reliable restaurant lists, skip general travel blogs and go straight to the source: the Korea Muslim Federation (KMF) website publishes its own list of certified halal restaurants, and apps like Zabihah and HappyCow (the second one is built for vegans and vegetarians, not halal, but is excellent for that purpose) let other travelers confirm a place is still open and still certified before you go.

For any dietary need, two apps are worth downloading before your trip: Naver Map (more accurate than Google Maps inside Korea, and locals use it too) and a translation app like Papago, which many Koreans also rely on when traveling abroad — it is genuinely better than most general translation apps for Korean food terms. Between an app that filters restaurants by diet and a translation app that can read a menu photo for you, you can handle almost any eating situation on your own.


Inside the Seoul Central Mosque, Itaewon — Korea's first mosque, open to visitors outside of prayer times. Photo by Toobigtokale via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Quick Comparison: Vegetarian, Vegan, and Halal in Korea

💬 Traveling with a specific diet and not sure what to order? Drop your situation in the comments — happy to help you figure it out before your trip!
meta_description: Beginner's guide to eating vegetarian, vegan, or halal in Korea: what to order, hidden ingredients to avoid, and where to find halal food in Seoul.
